tagline: From Big Pine into dry mountains where living trees exceed four millennia
intro: East of Big Pine, SR 168 climbs into the White Mountains through Westgard Pass. The mountains are arid desert, yet bristlecone and limber pines grow in this high country above views into Nevada’s Great Basin. The Forest Service highlights living trees more than 4,000 years old, with twisted, weathered wood. At Schulman Grove, trees are visible from the parking area and boardwalks, while self-guided trails offer a longer exploration. The visitor center opens in summer with interpretive programs on the trees.

The road over Westgard Pass predates numbered highways: it formed part of the Midland Trail, an early transcontinental automobile route. At Big Pine, westbound travelers divided toward Los Angeles or San Francisco. Later realignments moved the named trail away from this original SR 168 routing; present Midland Trail signs instead identify US 6 east toward Denver.

From Big Pine, the forest is reached by SR 168 and White Mountain Road, with the visitor center at Schulman Grove. Beyond Schulman, a dirt road continues 13 miles north to Patriarch Grove. The Forest Service says an early start allows a visit to both groves in one day. Food, water and fuel are back in Big Pine.
notice: Bristlecone and limber pines share the high landscape above views of Nevada’s Great Basin.

moments.title: Big Pine
moments.text: Big Pine sits between the Sierra Nevada and the White Mountains, beside the Owens River. It was also the Midland Trail’s branching point for westbound automobile journeys toward Los Angeles and San Francisco. At its road junction, a giant sequoia called the Roosevelt Pine commemorated the opening of Westgard Pass to automobile traffic in 1913. The tree was felled in September 2020 after its sole water source dried up during the 2017–18 drought. The town remains the nearest source of food, water and fuel for a visit to the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest.

moments.title: Schulman Grove
moments.text: Bristlecones can be seen from Schulman Grove’s parking area and the boardwalks beside the visitor center. That center replaces the building destroyed, with all its exhibits, by an arson fire in September 2008. The Forest Service describes a summer center offering interpretation and information on the trees. Self-guided trails lead farther into the forest, where living trees exceed 4,000 years. Methuselah, one of the forest’s ancient bristlecones, is unmarked to protect it from vandalism. Numbered natural-history markers along the Methuselah Grove trail are explained in a booklet, adding context to the walk.
moments.notice: Bristlecones are visible from the parking area and visitor-center boardwalks.

moments.title: Patriarch Grove
moments.text: Patriarch Grove lies 13 miles north of Schulman Grove along a dirt road. Here stands the Patriarch Tree, which the Forest Service identifies as the world’s largest bristlecone pine. The agency describes the grove’s appearance as a moonscape. Two short trails explore the grove, and a picnic area and restroom serve visitors. Both this grove and Schulman Grove are restricted to day use; the Forest Service requires hikers to stay on trails and prohibits collecting bristlecone or limber pine. The grove is also the source of Cottonwood Creek, a designated Wild and Scenic River.

practical: Patriarch Grove: The 13 miles beyond Schulman Grove are dirt road. Bring water and obtain food and fuel in Big Pine; cell coverage is limited. (checked 2026-10-11)
